name: Introduction to AI in Sports
objectives: Given examples of technology in sports, identify where AI is used in sports and what it cannot do for you, naming at least three uses and one limit

chapters.name: Chapter 1: Where AI shows up in sports

lessons.title: Lesson 1: What AI is, and where you already see it in sports
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Name three ways AI is used in sports today and say what AI cannot do.
This lesson builds toward: Given examples of technology in sports, you will identify where AI is used in sports and what it cannot do for you, naming at least three uses and one limit.
AI, or artificial intelligence, means computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person, like spotting patterns, writing text or recognizing what is in a video.
In sports you already see it: broadcasts that show a player's speed or a shot's chance of going in, apps that count your reps or track your runs, video tools that tag every play, and recruiting sites that sort athletes by stats.
AI is a helper, not a coach, doctor or referee. It does not know your body, your team or your goals unless you tell it, and it can be wrong. Coaches and athletes still make the calls.
Words to know:
- AI: short for artificial intelligence: programs that learn patterns from data and use them to answer, predict or create.
- Data: facts and numbers, like times, scores, reps or video.
Try it now: Write down three places you have seen AI or smart stats in your sport this season, for example a broadcast graphic, a fitness app or a video tool your team uses.
You can now explain what AI is, name three ways it shows up in sports, and say why people still make the decisions.

options: Computer programs that do tasks that usually need a person
check.why: AI means computer programs that spot patterns, write text or recognize what is in a video.

check.q: An AI app says you should change your position on the team. What do you do?
options: Talk with your coach; AI is a helper, not your coach
Ignore your coach from now on
check.why: AI does not know your team or goals; coaches and athletes still make the calls.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: Opening a free AI assistant
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Open a free AI assistant on your phone or a computer and send your first message.
This lesson builds toward: Using your phone or a computer, you will open a free AI assistant from its official app or website, send a first message and sign out on a shared computer, after checking the app's age rules.
An AI assistant is an AI program you chat with in everyday words. Well-known free ones are ChatGPT, Microsoft Copilot and Google Gemini.
On a phone, get the official app from the app store, made by the real company: OpenAI for ChatGPT, Microsoft for Copilot, Google for Gemini. On a computer, open a browser and go to chatgpt.com, copilot.microsoft.com or gemini.google.com.
Some assistants need an account and have age rules. If you are under 18, check the app's age rules and ask a parent or guardian first. On a school or shared computer, sign out when you finish.
Step by step:
- Pick your phone or a computer.
- Phone: install the official app. Computer: type the web address.
- Find the message box near the bottom of the screen.
- Type a hello message and read the answer.
- On a shared computer, sign out and close the browser.
Words to know:
- AI assistant: an AI program you chat with by typing or talking.
- Browser: the program you use to visit websites, like Chrome, Edge or Safari.
Try it now: Open one free AI assistant and type: "I play [your sport]. Explain in three short sentences how AI is used in my sport." Read the answer.
You can now open a free AI assistant, send a message and leave a shared computer safely.

check.q: Which web address opens Google Gemini on a computer?
check.why: gemini.google.com is the official address; use the real company's site or app.

check.q: You used ChatGPT on a library computer to plan your week. What do you do when you finish?
options: Leave it open for a teammate
Sign out and close the browser
check.why: Signing out on shared computers keeps others out of your chats and accounts.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: Writing a clear sports prompt
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Write a prompt with your need, your situation and the format you want.
This lesson builds toward: Given your real practice, game and class schedule, you will write a prompt with your need, your situation and the format you want, so the first answer is useful.
What you type to an AI assistant is called a prompt. A clear prompt gets a useful answer the first time.
A strong prompt has three parts: what you need, your situation, and how you want the answer. Example: "I am a high school soccer midfielder. I have practice Monday to Thursday 3:30 to 5:30 and a game Friday. Make a simple study schedule for the week around practice. Put it in a table."
A weak prompt like "help me get better" makes the assistant guess. Add the sport, the position, your schedule and the format.
Step by step:
- Say what you need.
- Add your sport, position, level and schedule (no private details).
- Say the format: list, table, short steps or simple words.
Words to know:
- Prompt: what you type or say to an AI assistant to ask for something.
- Format: the shape of the answer, like a list, a table or steps.
Try it now: Write a three-part prompt asking for a study or recovery-day schedule around your real practice week. Send it and read the answer.
You can now write a clear sports prompt that includes your need, your situation and the format.

check.q: What is the format part of a prompt?
options: How you want the answer, like a table or a short list
check.why: The format tells the assistant how to shape the answer.

check.q: You want help planning homework around basketball. Which prompt is best?
options: "I'm a high school guard with practice 3 to 5 pm Monday to Thursday and a game Friday. Make a homework schedule for the week in a table."
check.why: It gives the need, the situation and the format.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Making the answer better
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 4 minutes
Goal: Use follow-up prompts to fix an answer until it fits your week.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer that does not fit your week, you will ask follow-up prompts, one change at a time, to fix it, making at least two improvements.
The first answer is a draft. The assistant remembers what you said earlier in the same chat, so you can ask for changes.
Useful follow-ups for athletes: "Move study time after dinner on game days." "Make it shorter." "Add a rest day." "Use simpler words." "Explain why you put this here."
Ask for one change at a time. If the chat goes off track, start a new chat with a clearer prompt.
Step by step:
- Read the first answer.
- Find what does not fit your real schedule.
- Ask for one change.
- Repeat until it fits.
Words to know:
- Follow-up: a second request that builds on the answer you got.
Try it now: Take your schedule from Lesson 3. Ask for two changes, one at a time, so it matches your real week. Compare the first and last versions.
You can now improve an AI answer with clear follow-up prompts.

check.q: Why can you ask the assistant to change its answer?
options: It remembers what you said earlier in the same chat
check.why: In the same chat the assistant remembers earlier messages, so you can ask for changes.

check.q: The plan puts heavy study time right before your Friday game. What do you send?
options: "Move study time on game day to after dinner."
check.why: A clear follow-up that names one change fixes the plan.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Checking AI answers with your coach
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Spot the parts of an AI answer that need checking and check them with the right person or source.
This lesson builds toward: Given an AI answer with training, health, nutrition or eligibility advice, you will check it with your coach, athletic trainer, dietitian, doctor, compliance office or an official page, before you follow it.
AI can make things up or give old information. This is sometimes called a hallucination. In sports, that could be a wrong rule, a made-up stat, an old recruiting date or unsafe training advice.
Always check training loads, injury and health advice, nutrition, supplements, eligibility, recruiting and NIL rules. Check with your coach, athletic trainer, doctor, registered dietitian, or your school's compliance office, and with official pages like ncaa.org.
A good habit: ask the assistant "What should I double-check with my coach?" Then actually ask your coach.
Step by step:
- Mark every fact, number, rule or health tip in the answer.
- Decide who should check it: coach, athletic trainer, doctor, dietitian or compliance office.
- Check official pages for rules.
- If they disagree, follow the person or the official source.
Words to know:
- Hallucination: when an AI writes something that sounds true but is made up.
- Compliance office: the school office that knows the athletic rules, including recruiting and NIL rules.
Official sources:
- NCAA: Name, Image and Likeness (rules for college athletes)
Try it now: Ask an AI assistant one rule question about your sport, for example how many timeouts each team gets. Then find the answer in your league's official rulebook or ask your coach, and see if it matches.
You can now spot what needs checking in an AI answer and take it to the right person or official source.

options: Something the AI makes up that sounds true
check.why: AI can make up rules, stats or dates that sound real.

check.q: The AI suggests a supplement to recover faster. Who checks it?
options: A registered dietitian, your doctor or your athletic trainer
check.why: Supplements and nutrition advice must be checked with the right professional, and with compliance for eligibility.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping your private and health information safe
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Use AI for a real task without sharing private, health or account information.
This lesson builds toward: When you write a prompt or get an offer online, you will keep private and health details out and spot scams aimed at athletes, sharing no passwords, codes, ID numbers or health records.
Do not type private details into an AI assistant: passwords, Social Security or ID numbers, your home address, bank details, or health records like injury reports, medications or test results.
You can still get help. Write "[my school]" or "a hamstring injury my athletic trainer is treating" instead of names and medical details. Ask general questions; bring the specific ones to the professional.
Watch out for scams aimed at athletes: fake recruiters, fake brand deals and fake agents who rush you, ask for money up front or ask for a login code. Check them with your coach or compliance office first.
Step by step:
- Read your prompt before you send it.
- Take out names, numbers, passwords and health details.
- Use placeholders like "[my school]".
- Treat rushed offers, upfront fees and code requests as warning signs.
Words to know:
- Placeholder: a stand-in like "[my school]" that keeps the real detail private.
- Scam: a trick to steal money, accounts or information.
Try it now: Final task: build your one-week practice-and-study plan with an AI assistant. Use a three-part prompt, ask for two improvements, remove private and health details, and show the plan to your coach or athletic trainer.
You can now use AI to plan your week while keeping private and health information safe, and spot scams aimed at athletes.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Clear prompt The prompt is vague, such as "make me a plan". The prompt gives the need, your real practice, game and class schedule, and the format. The first answer already fits most of your week. Made it better Used the first answer as it was. Asked for at least two improvements, one at a time. Can say what each change fixed, such as a rest day or game-day timing. Private and health details out The prompt has a name, ID number, password or health detail. No private or health details in the prompt or plan. Used placeholders like "[my school]" and kept health questions for the athletic trainer. Checked with coach Followed the plan without showing anyone. Showed the plan to your coach or athletic trainer before following it. Changed the plan based on their feedback and can say what changed. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: Which detail should you keep out of a prompt?
options: Your injury report and medication list
check.why: Health records like injury reports and medications stay out of AI tools.

check.q: An "agent" messages you with a brand deal and asks for a login code to finish today. What do you do?
options: Never share the code, and check with your coach or compliance office
Pay the fee to hold the deal
check.why: Rushing you and asking for a code are warning signs of a scam.
